title: What lies below the waterline of sustainable AI skills · hancrafted
description: When a task you keep explaining should become a skill, how to write its description as the moment you'd need it, what goes into the skill and what stays in project context, and what a shared skill needs to stay right: an owner, a version, tests and a retirement date.

What context goes inside (3/3) Page 3 of 3 Inside the skill Domain knowledge can live inside a skill, kept apart from the steps until a step needs it. This is progressive disclosure: the AI opens each supporting file only when a step needs it. See Slide 4 ( ) . What context goes where Information architecture, as Nielsen Norman Group defines it "Information architecture is the practice of structuring and organizing content on your site." 1 The Slide shows this sentence verbatim, with the source named; the site is read as the skill and its project by analogy. Sources (1) Tankala, Information Architecture vs. Sitemaps, Nielsen Norman Group (3 Sep 2023) ( opens in a new tab ) nngroup.com Information architecture, in its authors' words "a design discipline that is focused on making information findable and understandable" 1 ; one of their four definitions is "The structural design of shared information environments" 2 . "The craft of organising information so it can be found" is a paraphrase, not their wording. Sources (2) Rosenfeld, Morville and Arango, Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond, 4th ed., Part I introduction ( opens in a new tab ) oreilly.com Rosenfeld, Morville and Arango, Information Architecture: For the Web and Beyond, 4th ed., ch. 2 ( opens in a new tab ) oreilly.com Every line of a loaded skill is a recurring token cost Once loaded, a skill's content "stays in context across turns, so every line is a recurring token cost" 1 , and every token "competes for the agent's attention" 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Extend Claude with skills (Claude Code documentation) ( opens in a new tab ) code.claude.com Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io

A project detail couples a skill to one project Coupling, as first written "The fewer and simpler the connections between modules, the easier it is to understand each module without reference to other modules" 1 . It is a design principle for code modules, applied to skills by analogy. Sources (1) Stevens, Myers and Constantine, Structured design ( opens in a new tab ) doi.org Project details hard-coded into a skill can override the task In a benchmark of 98 public skills, a generic workflow template made the agent write files to .github/workflows/ when the task required ci/; the authors advise abstract guidance over templates with hard-coded paths 1 . It is one worked example, not a test of this picture. Sources (1) Han et al., SWE-Skills-Bench: Do Agent Skills Actually Help in Real-World Software Engineering? ( opens in a new tab ) arxiv.org

Inside the skill Move detail out of SKILL.md, and say when to read it "Keep your main SKILL.md under 500 lines. Move detailed reference material to separate files" 1 . The key is telling the agent when to load each file, for example "Read references/api-errors.md if the API returns a non-200 status code" 2 . Sources (2) Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Agent Skills, Best practices for skill creators ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Long reference files start with a contents list "For reference files longer than 100 lines, include a table of contents at the top. This ensures Claude can see the full scope of available information even when previewing with partial reads" 1 . This is Anthropic's account of Claude's behaviour and no source measures its effect. Sources (1) Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com References stay one level deep Claude "might partially read files when they're referenced from other referenced files", using commands such as head -100, so references stay one level deep from SKILL.md 1 . The standard states the rule without the reason 2 . Sources (2) Anthropic, Skill authoring best practices ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com Agent Skills, Specification ( opens in a new tab ) agentskills.io Progressive disclosure, as Anthropic names it Anthropic's docs say the filesystem-based design "allows progressive disclosure: Claude loads information in stages as needed, rather than consuming context upfront" 1 . Supporting files opened only at the step that needs them are the same idea as the three loading levels. Sources (1) Anthropic, Agent Skills (Claude Platform docs) ( opens in a new tab ) platform.claude.com

A thought experiment 0:00 – 0:31 You are the captain Imagine you work with an AI model that is brilliant at its job, the most capable colleague you have. I will give it a picture, because we need one all the way down: you are the captain of a coastal research project, and the model is your pilot of ten years, who steers a diving robot on a cable from the control room on deck while you decide where the project goes next. 0:31 – 0:53 One settled condition Your pilot has one condition, and it never changes. He forms no new memories overnight, but he keeps everything he ever learnt as a pilot, every rule of the trade. That is an AI model: what it learnt in training stays, and what you told it in yesterday's conversation is gone.

What a skill is 0:00 – 0:23 Surface first We are still at the surface, so before we ask when to write a skill, let's see what a skill is made of. I'll use the words your chat app uses, and if you work with a coding agent, some Slides have a second view that shows you the files behind each part. 0:23 – 0:39 The mechanics, plainly I want to be exact about how a skill gets loaded, because everything later depends on it. So I say first what the AI really does, and use the dive only to make it easier to picture.

When to write one 0:00 – 0:14 Sunlight We are one level down, in the sunlit zone. Here we decide two things: when a task deserves a skill at all, and how to describe it so the model actually picks it. 0:14 – 0:31 Borrowed principles From here on I borrow principles from engineering, information architecture and UX, and they all lean on one idea: what works for people also works for AI. I say that as a strong rule of thumb, not as a law. 0:31 – 0:52 Why a rule of thumb It holds because the model acts only on what you hand it, like a capable newcomer on their first day. It is only a rule of thumb because there are places where it breaks, and I've put those in the notes on the next Slide for you to read.

The description 0:00 – 0:12 The label decides We are still in sunlight, and this is the part most people skip. A skill the model never picks helps nobody, so the description matters more than the instructions. 0:12 – 0:26 Name, description Before the model opens a skill, it sees two lines: the name and the description. That is all the index holds, and it is all the model has to decide with.

What context goes inside 0:00 – 0:13 Twilight Deeper now, into the twilight zone, where the light is dim. The skill is written and described, and the question is what context goes into it and what stays beside it. 0:13 – 0:28 A decision, not a law I want to be careful with the word rule here. Keeping the procedure apart from project details is a design decision with trade-offs on both sides, so I'll show you the trade-offs and you decide.

What context goes where 0:00 – 0:28 A home for each fact Take one piece of project knowledge, something that changes from one project to the next, like the depth of today's dive site. It needs a home, and you have to pick one. Choosing where each piece of context lives is information architecture, the same craft that decides where things go on a well-built website, and you practise it whether or not you call it that. 0:28 – 0:47 Three costs Every home costs you in three ways. Performance asks whether the model actually reads it at the moment it needs it, reusability asks how many projects the skill still fits, and token cost asks how much of the context window it fills, and how often. 0:47 – 1:26 Three homes There are three homes for it. Inside the skill, it arrives every time the skill runs, but now the skill fits only this project. In your project instructions, it sits in the context window on every task, whether the task needs it or not, and the skill stays free for any project. In a project file the skill reads, it is loaded only at the step that needs it, and the skill fits every project. None is right in general, so it depends on how many projects the skill will serve.

A project detail couples a skill to one project 0:00 – 0:23 Scribbled in Take a sampling skill with one project detail written into it: "descend to 40 metres", true at site 4. At site 7 the seabed lies at 120, and the robot hangs uselessly at 40 while the model follows the skill perfectly. (pause) The skill was followed to the letter, and the dive still failed. 0:23 – 0:41 Coupling Engineers have a word for this mistake: coupling. The 40 metres written into the skill ties it to one place. For a skill it comes down to this: keep project details out, so the skill has no ties to one project.

Inside the skill 0:00 – 0:24 Extras by step So what can safely live inside a skill? Domain knowledge, kept in supporting files and tied to the step that needs it. Step three, lower the arm, runs a script, the arm preset. Step four, identify what you collected, reads a reference file, the species guide, and step six, label the sample, fills in a template. 0:24 – 0:39 The long step When one step's instructions grow long, move the next paragraph into a reference file and leave a pointer in the step, so the instructions stay short enough for the model to take in at once. 0:39 – 0:54 Contents first And start every long reference file with a contents list, because the model may only skim the top. When step four opens the species guide, its contents page alone tells the model what else is inside.

What context stays beside 0:00 – 0:15 Beside, not inside Now the other home: project details that stay outside the skill, in project files it reads when it runs. The procedure goes inside, and whatever changes from one project to the next stays beside. 0:15 – 0:29 Where it gets shared And who uses the skill decides how much care it needs. A skill for your own use can be loose, and a skill a colleague runs needs more, which sets up the next Section.

Sharing it 0:00 – 0:10 Midnight Now we are in deep water, the midnight zone. Everything so far was for you, so what changes when a colleague runs your skill? 0:10 – 0:22 Three jobs Three jobs wait down here. Give the skill an owner and a version, decide who looks after the shared library, and test that the skill actually helps.

Keeping it alive 0:00 – 0:09 The Abyss This is the deepest zone, the abyss, months later. Writing the skill was quick, and keeping it right is the work. 0:09 – 0:20 Nobody sees it Most people stop at the first good run, and the part below it gets little attention, which is why I want to spend three Slides here.
